A perfect cadence closes a phrase by moving from the dominant chord to the tonic.
A half cadence ends a phrase on the dominant chord, leaving the music poised to continue.
A deceptive cadence sends the dominant to an unexpected chord, usually the chord on the sixth degree, delaying the close.
A plagal cadence moves from the subdominant chord to the tonic, as in many settings of ‘Amen’.
Elision overlaps the end of one musical phrase or section with the beginning of the next.
A pivot chord belongs to both the old key and the new one, helping the music pass between them.
Common-tone modulation connects keys through a note that belongs to both the departing and arriving harmonies.
Direct modulation moves into a new key without a connecting passage or pivot chord.
Enharmonic reinterpretation gives a note or chord a new spelling and harmonic role while keeping its sounding pitch.
A chromatic slide shifts a note or chord by a semitone into a new harmonic setting.
A sequence repeats a melodic or harmonic pattern at successively higher or lower pitches.
A dominant pedal holds or repeats the fifth note of the key while the music above it changes.
A tonic pedal holds or repeats the home note while the chords and melodies around it move.
A retransition leads back from a contrasting passage to the return of familiar opening music.
Standing on the dominant prolongs dominant harmony while the melody and rhythm continue to move.
Liquidation gradually removes a motif’s distinctive features until only a simple figure or chord remains.
